newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU leaders duck key hurdle to new treaty.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders duck key hurdle to new treaty.

text.p: European Union leaders ducked a key hurdle to a new treaty on Tuesday by postponing a decision on changing the balance of power in the 15-nation bloc until a planned expansion into eastern Europe early next century.

The decision on changing the EU's weighted majority voting system was deferred after a deadlock between big countries seeking more votes in line with their population, and smaller states clinging to historic over-representation.
"There is an agreement on the institutions, in the sense that they (member states) will decide what to do at the moment of enlargement," a senior EU official said.

Two days of horse-trading that saw national sensitivities derail a number of agreements sought by European integrationists preceded a difficult session between large and small EU countries over their clout.

The argument got bitter with Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene angrily saying the carve-up proposed by the Dutch presidency would give the Netherlands more votes than Belgium, its neighbour and Benelux partner, diplomats said.

Spain protested that it would be detached from the group of big countries. Eventually German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said there was no chance of agreement, so the issue should be kicked into touch to enable the rest of the treaty to be approved.
"There is no appetite to get into this stuff. It makes them angry and hopping mad," a diplomat said.
The fight centred on a demand by the bloc's large countries to recoup some of the power in decision-making that they lost through the arrival of newcomers such as Sweden and Finland.
The issue is considered crucial by the bloc's powers as the EU plans to bring in as many as a dozen new and relatively small members from eastern Europe.
Under the agreement, the bloc's five largest countries would be asked to give up one of their two European commissioners upon enlargement to limit the size of the Brussels executive to 20.
Most progress on Tuesday came by diluting earlier proposals.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark were given opt-outs from parts of the treaty in a move that leaders hoped would prompt closer cooperation in crime fighting and immigration policy.

London and Dublin would retain their borders and the right to set their own visa, immigration and asylum policy. Copenhagen's opt-out reflects constitutional problems with passing sovereignty to EU institutions.
France settled for the appointment of a senior, but relatively obscure, Eurocrat to take on the task of coordinating EU foreign policy, deferring for now on its desire for a high-profile candidate.
National sensitivities, meanwhile, ensured that the veto would remain in areas of immigration and refugee policy while Germany made sure it was extended to asylum policy, too.
The move was a blow to those who have argued over the 15 months of talks that majority voting is necessary for the bloc to be effective.

Under the latest draft treaty, EU countries would agree to cooperate more closely in areas such as asylum, immigration, visa policy and crime fighting. Breaking from current practice, the European Commission would be allowed to recommend rules.
The Schengen accord, linking most of the bloc's members in a partially completed border-free zone, would also be incorporated into the EU, lifting frontiers throughout the continent.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark would be given various opt-outs to meet their internal political concerns.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair, as unbending in some areas as his predecessors if not as strident, vetoed plans to bring the Western European Union (WEU) into the EU over time, leaving the treaty's text on defence saying simply that incorporation was a possibility.
With one eye on the citizens they are seeking to court, the leaders have also agreed that an Employment Chapter should be put into the treaty to raise job creation high in the agenda.
